newsitem.title: FRANCE: Dry weather may crimp French grain yields - source.
newsitem.headline: Dry weather may crimp French grain yields - source.

text.p: Dry weather in France has begun to put stress on winter cereals crops, raising fears of some loss in yields if rain does not come in the next 10 days, a French agriculture ministry source said on Tuesday.
The source did not hazard a guess at how badly yields could be affected, but said water shortage in the top soil was already affecting stems of winter wheat and reducing the number of ears.
However French wheat growers' association AGPB, while noting the potential risk from drought, said it was too soon to say how crops would perform between now and the summer harvest.
"It is extremely dry. There are problems. The crops are suffering from lack of water," the farm ministry source said.
French weather service Meteo France predicted dry weather nationally throughout the week with cooler temperatures and possible frost in some areas over the weekend.
Autumn-sown crops, which lie dormant through the winter and are harvested in mid-summer, make up about 90 percent of the French wheat crop, Europe's largest and a major French export earner.
They also make up 70 percent of the French barley crop.
Farmers had boosted their sowings of winter grain to take advantage of a reduction in the amount of land they have to leave idle under European Union (EU) planting restrictions.
But a drop in yields would limit the increase in actual production.

Yet grain experts are wary of predicting the impact on output after France managed to reap a record 34.7 million tonnes of wheat last year despite drought in western Europe's largest grain belt, the Beauce region south of Paris.
Analysts had to hike their forecasts last summer after an unexpected surge in yields elsewhere, mainly in the north.
Nonetheless the French ministry source said a certain amount of damage now had to be built in to industry forecasts.
"In a general sense winter crops can still start catching up if it rains, but they are going to be penalised anyway," he said.
French winter wheat yields rose on average last year to 7.27 tonnes per hectare from 6.61 tonnes in 1995, while winter barley yielded 6.35 tonnes compared with 5.89 tonnes in 1995.
However higher grain yields, while filling farmers' bins, can reduce quality and raise the proportion of crops suitable only for animal feed rather than higher-value food processing.
Latest farm ministry statistics point to an increase in the area of winter wheat sowings to 6.63 million hectares for the 1997 harvest from 6.41 million tonnes last year.
The next estimate will be published in mid-April.
A spokeswoman for the AGPB said dry spells were generally bad for yields but stressed there had been similar fears last year before farmers produced an exceptional crop.
"In 1996 people thought there would be a mediocre harvest but everything swung round in July," she said.
"We don't want to say anything now. It's too soon. Let's wait until the end of June or July," she added.
Last year's false alarm over grain production briefly prompted the EU Commission to delay giving new export subsidies.
The French ministry source said there were also some concerns over spring sowings of wheat and barley, as well as sunflowers used for vegetable oil and animal feed.
The young crops need water to get started and some farmers have been turning up the taps in their irrigation systems.
But fears of another drought have prompted several provinces in central France to impose curbs on artificial watering.
"The ground is well prepared but it needs humidity to make the grain germinate," the ministry source said.
Maize or corn, exclusively spring-sown and a quarter of the annual French grain harvest, has yet to go in the ground but could be affected if water shortages persist, the source said.
Ironically, however, part of the pasta-making durum wheat crop has had to be resown because of flooding last autumn.
--Paule Bonjean, Paris newsroom +331 4221 5146
